opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That paper is a good example because it started from a question that everyone was arguing about but nobody had really pinned down. Around the time GPT-3 came out, there was this big debate: are prompts actually doing something meaningful, or are they just a hack that works at enormous scale? And people had strong intuitions on both sides, but the arguments were mostly anecdotal.

What Teven Le Scao and I wanted to do was turn that into something you could measure. The core idea was really simple: take a standard classification setup, compare fine-tuning a model with a head on top versus fine-tuning with a prompt that frames the task in natural language, and then ask, how much extra training data does the non-prompted model need to catch up? So instead of saying "prompting helps," you can say something like "a prompt is worth on the order of hundreds of data points" for a given task. That gives you a unit, a kind of exchange rate, and suddenly the conversation becomes much more concrete.

I love that style of research for a few reasons. One, it's small. You don't need a giant compute budget; you need a clean question and a careful experimental design. Two, it's the kind of thing where the framing is the contribution. Ideally, once you see the framing, it feels almost obvious, and you think, why didn't we measure it this way before? And three, it tends to age well. Models change, methods change, but having a way to quantify the value of something like a prompt gives people a tool they can keep reusing.

Honestly, a lot of my favorite work is like that: not inventing a fancy new architecture, but taking a fuzzy debate in the community and finding the right lens so we can actually reason about it.

r001.rationale: It describes measuring how much additional training data a model without a prompt needs to catch up, giving the prompt an equivalent value in data points.

r002.rationale: It identifies this style of research as a favorite and describes a clean question with careful experimental design.

r003.rationale: It says a prompt can be worth hundreds of data points for a task, but does not state that writing down the task reduces annotation needs at small training-data scales.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about whether writing down the task is worthwhile at large training-data scales.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I love about that paper is that it's a small question with a really precise answer. It started with a kind of nagging feeling that everyone had been having for a while, which was that these pretrained models were working really well, and people had started doing this thing where you write a little template, a prompt, and sort of reframe your classification task as fill-in-the-blank. And the folklore was that this helps, especially when you don't have much data. But nobody had actually tried to quantify it. So Teven and I just sat down and asked, okay, if a prompt helps, how much does it help, and can we put that in units that people already understand? And the unit we landed on was data points. You can draw the learning curve for the model with a prompt and the learning curve without one, and the horizontal gap between those curves is basically how many labeled examples the prompt is buying you. That number turned out to be in the hundreds for a lot of tasks, which was surprising to me. I expected a modest effect.

What makes it the kind of research I like is that it's cheap, it's empirical, and it's falsifiable. We didn't propose a new architecture, we didn't need enormous compute, it was mostly careful experiments and a plot that anyone can look at and immediately get. I'm drawn to work where the contribution is a clean way of measuring something rather than a new system. And I think the field often undervalues that. A lot of the interesting questions in NLP right now are really about understanding what these models already know and how to get it out of them, and you don't need a thousand GPUs to make progress on that. You need a good question and a controlled experiment.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a very honest paper. We tried the obvious counterarguments, like whether the template actually matters or whether it's just the extra parameters, whether a nonsense prompt does as well, and some of those results were a bit humbling. The prompt wording mattered less than I expected in some cases. But that's the fun part. You go in with a hypothesis, the data tells you something slightly different, and you report it. That's the loop I enjoy, and it's one that students can actually do end-to-end, which matters a lot to me as someone who spends most of my time working with students.

r001.rationale: It says the prompt’s benefit was measured in data points, as the number of labeled examples the prompt is “buying you.”

r002.rationale: It describes Sasha’s preferred research as answering a small, precise question with careful, controlled empirical experiments.

r003.rationale: It says prompts can help especially when there is little data and quantifies that benefit as hundreds of labeled examples.

r004.rationale: It does not state that prompts might be less worthwhile for reducing annotation needs when training data is large.

astra-6.text:
What I like about that question is that it takes something people are excited about—prompting—and asks for a concrete way to understand it. If I spend time writing a better prompt, how does that compare to giving the model more labeled examples? Can we put those two ways of improving a system on the same scale?

That’s the kind of research I really enjoy: a simple question where designing the comparison carefully is a big part of the intellectual work. You’re not just asking whether one method gets a higher score. You’re trying to understand what it buys you, and under what circumstances. And even if the answer turns out to depend on the task or the model, you’ve made the discussion more precise.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether prompting and labeled examples can be put on the same scale, but does not state that the study quantified task descriptions as an equivalent number of supervised examples.

r002.rationale: It says Sasha enjoys a simple question with a carefully designed comparison, but does not clearly identify a narrowly defined empirical question answered through carefully controlled experiments.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that writing down the task reduced annotation needs at small training-data scales.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that writing down the task might not reduce annotation needs at large training-data scales.

sol-6.1.text:
I like research that starts with a really simple question that turns out to be surprisingly hard to answer. Here the question is: if I give a model a good prompt, how much labeled training data is that actually buying me? Can I put those two things on the same scale?

Because we say things like, “This prompt works really well,” but that doesn’t give you much of a sense of how valuable it is. Comparing it to additional data gives you a concrete way to think about that. And it forces you to ask what happens as you change the amount of data, rather than just comparing two methods at one particular point.

That’s the kind of work I really enjoy: take something people are doing, find a basic question underneath it, and design an experiment that makes the answer clearer. It doesn’t have to introduce a more complicated model. Sometimes the contribution is giving people a better way to understand what they already have.
